newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus's economy is sound, finance minister says.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus's economy is sound, finance minister says.

text.p: Cyprus's finance minister dismissed on Thursday criticism of government policies from opposition parties, saying the economy was far better off now than five years ago.
Finance Minister Christodoulos Christodoulou blasted opposition members of parliament who attacked fiscal policies during a three day budget debate in parliament.

Left-wing opposition party MPs said the current centre-right government had increased taxes, caused higher unemployment, depressed growth rates to record lows and spurred increases in the public deficit.
"I thought they (the speakers) were addressing residents of another country," the minister told a news conference, accusing the opposition of campaigning for the 1998 presidential poll.
The minister said the International Monetary Fund had given Cyprus's economy a clean bill of health in its last 1996 report, as had international rating agencies.
Presidential elections, held every five years, are due in early 1998. Current President Glafcos Clerides has not confirmed whether he plans to stand for re-election.

"Economy is to a great extent psychology...if this psychology is wounded and if feelings of lack of trust are created, then this economy cannot but be affected as far as its behaviour is concerned," said Christodoulou.

Finance ministry data put the fiscal deficit forecast at an average of 2.4 percent of gross national product (GDP) in the five years of the Clerides administration, in contrast to 5.0 percent of the previous administration under Vassiliou.
Most of the minister's ire was directed at Vassiliou, now chairman of the United Democrats party, whose candidature in next year's elections also hangs in the balance.
Vassiliou said last year's rate of GDP growth, 2.5 percent, was the worst in years.
"The worst rate growth was in 1991, of 0.6 percent and that accomplishment belongs to Mr. Vassiliou," Christodoulou said.
He said the island was fully on course with aligning its economy to that of the European Union, which it is due to start entry talks with next year.
Public debt excluding intragovernmental, as defined by the Maastricht Treaty, is forecast at 54.2 of GDP in 1997 compared to preliminary estimates of 54.1 percent for 1996.

GDP growth of 3.5 percent is expected compared with estimates of 2.5 percent in 1996. Inflation is forecast at 3.0 percent, the same as last year, while unemployment is forecast to hover at the same levels.
